samples.summary: The CLI login URL — which carries the whole nonce + PKCE challenge pair — is handed to `open()`, i.e. placed in a child process's argv, where any local user can read it and defeat all three new loopback bindings
samples.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` (login.ts:199) goes to great lengths to keep the authorization URL off stderr because "anyone who reads it can start their own login against the same pair and push the resulting code at this port", and writes it 0600 when stderr is not a TTY. But `openBrowser` (login.ts:176-184) passes the same URL to `open(url)`, which spawns `xdg-open <url>` / `open <url>` / a powershell shim with the URL as a command-line argument. On Linux with the default `hidepid=0` /proc (and on macOS via `ps`), any other local user sees `mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>&code_challenge=<challenge>` in full. Attack: local attacker reads the URL from `ps`; opens `https://server/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim's port>&nonce=<victim's nonce>&code_challenge=<victim's challenge>` in their own browser and consents as themselves; the backend mints a code bound to the copied challenge and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<victim port>/callback?code=A&state=<victim nonce>` — the same loopback the victim's CLI is listening on. The CLI's `nonceMatches` (login.ts:331) passes because the nonce was copied, and `POST /auth/cli/exchange` succeeds because the victim's verifier hashes to the copied challenge (cli-auth.store.ts:136). The victim's terminal is now logged into the attacker's account and every subsequent `wafflebase` write lands in the attacker's workspace — exactly the RFC 8252 §8.9 injection this change claims to close, on the multi-user host the change's own docs put in scope (docs/design/cli.md 'Browser binding').

samples.summary: Anyone can start a `mode=cli` login pointing at an arbitrary loopback port; the new browser-binding cookie does not stop the start-URL variant of the phishing attack it is documented as closing
samples.evidence: `GET /auth/github` is unauthenticated and accepts `mode=cli&port=<any 1024-65535>&nonce=<attacker's>&code_challenge=<attacker's>` from any origin (github-auth.guard.ts:98-129). The browser-binding cookie only rules out an attacker *pre-minting* a state in their own browser and replaying the callback; it does nothing when the attacker simply gets the victim to click the crafted **start** URL — the victim's own browser then mints the cookie, passes `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:190-200), and the server redirects the victim to `http://127.0.0.1:<attacker-chosen port>/callback?code=<victim's code>&state=<attacker's nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:145). Because the attacker chose the `code_challenge`, they hold the verifier, so PKCE does not protect the code either: an attacker with any listener on the victim's loopback (shared/multi-user host, or a malicious local helper) redeems the victim's code at `/auth/cli/exchange` and receives the victim's access + refresh tokens. The guard comment (github-auth.guard.ts:76-81) and the risk row in docs/design/rest-api.md:399 both assert the cookie closes 'an attacker mints a CLI state pointing at a loopback port they own and walks the victim through consent', which is only true for the callback-replay variant — a control that reads as covered but is not.

samples.summary: The browser-flow CSRF defense is an unsigned double-submit cookie with a `Domain`-settable name, so a sibling-subdomain cookie injection still yields forced-login CSRF
samples.evidence: `issueStateCookie` sets `wafflebase_oauth_state` with `httpOnly/sameSite=lax/path=/auth` but no integrity binding, no `__Host-`/`__Secure-` name prefix, and `secure` only when NODE_ENV==='production'. `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:179-188) accepts any callback where the presented `w.<value>` equals the cookie value. An attacker who controls or XSSes any sibling subdomain (or, in a non-production deployment, an on-path attacker over plain HTTP) can set `wafflebase_oauth_state=X; Domain=.<site>; Path=/auth` in the victim's browser and then navigate the victim to `/auth/github/callback?code=<attacker's GitHub code>&state=w.X`. Both halves match, so the victim's browser is issued `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` for the attacker's account — the forced-login CSRF this change is meant to close. Signing/HMACing the cookie value against the state, or a `__Host-`-prefixed cookie, would remove the injection path.

samples.summary: A callback with no `state` at all is rejected without clearing the `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie, so the pending login half stays spendable
samples.evidence: `verifyCallbackState` calls `takeStateCookie` (which clears the cookie) on both the `w.`-prefixed branch and the CLI branch, but the final `throw new UnauthorizedException` at auth.controller.ts:210 runs without touching the cookie. A callback deliberately stripped of `state` therefore leaves the victim's live state cookie in place for its full 5-minute lifetime, contradicting the 'single use, cleared whether or not it matched' invariant the surrounding comments (lines 216-219) and docs/design/rest-api.md:355 state. Low direct impact, but it is the one path where the documented clearing does not happen.

samples.summary: `login-url.txt` is written into a directory that may be attacker-writable (WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG-derived), with an rm-then-write TOCTOU and no cleanup if the process dies
samples.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` builds the path from `dirname(getConfigPath())`, which is fully controlled by `WAFFLEBASE_CONFIG` (config.ts:56) and may sit in a shared directory such as /tmp in CI. `rmSync(file, {force:true})` followed by `writeFileSync(file, url, {mode:0o600})` leaves a window in which a local attacker can re-create the path as a symlink, so the login URL (nonce + PKCE challenge, i.e. the full binding pair per the finding above) is written through to an attacker-readable location. Additionally the file is only removed in the `finally` of the callback wait (login.ts:72); a SIGKILL or crash leaves a live 5-minute login secret on disk. `writeFileSync` with `flag: 'wx'` after the unlink, or an O_NOFOLLOW open, would close the symlink window.

samples.summary: `createState` is reachable unauthenticated and the in-memory state map is only pruned opportunistically, so `/auth/github?mode=cli...` is a cheap memory-growth vector
samples.evidence: Every unauthenticated `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=1024&nonce=n&code_challenge=<43 base64url chars>` inserts a 5-minute `StateEntry` (github-auth.guard.ts:121, cli-auth.store.ts:66). `cleanup()` only sweeps entries already past TTL, so a distributed flood under the 120 req/min/IP global throttle accumulates unbounded live entries. Pre-existing in shape, but the change adds three more stored strings per entry and makes the CLI start path the only one that mints them. A per-IP cap or a hard map-size ceiling would bound it.

finding.summary: CLI OAuth `state` is not bound to the browser that started the flow, so an attacker who can bind a loopback port on the victim's machine can capture the victim's authorization code
finding.evidence:
The change adds a browser binding for the web flow (a `w.`-prefixed state whose other half is the `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie, github-auth.guard.ts:128-139, checked at auth.controller.ts:174-188) but the CLI branch (github-auth.guard.ts:105-111) mints a bare store-backed token with no cookie and no per-browser binding, and auth.controller.ts:190-194 accepts it from ANY browser.

Vector: (1) the attacker binds 127.0.0.1:P on a shared host / container / multi-user dev box the victim also uses; (2) the attacker calls `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=P&nonce=N&code_challenge=C` themselves and reads `state=S` straight out of their own 302 `Location` header — the endpoint is unauthenticated, so S is free; (3) the attacker phishes the victim with `https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=…&state=S`; the victim (already having authorized the app) is silently redirected to `/auth/github/callback?code=<victim's GitHub code>&state=S`; (4) `verifyCallbackState` finds S in the CLI store and returns it, `findOrCreateUser` resolves to the **victim**, and auth.controller.ts:140-149 redirects the victim's browser to `http://127.0.0.1:P/callback?code=<code>&state=N` — the attacker's listener; (5) the attacker redeems the code at `POST /auth/cli/exchange` with the verifier V they chose in step 2 and receives the victim's access + refresh tokens.

The nonce echo does not help (the attacker picked N) and PKCE does not help (the attacker picked C and holds V). The `state` echo protects the CLI *from* injected codes; nothing protects the *server* from a CLI state replayed in an unrelated browser. The natural fix is to give the CLI state the same cookie half the web state now gets (or to require the CLI's own confirmation of the browser that started it).

verdict.reason: The finding claims the CLI OAuth `state` is minted with no cookie and no per-browser binding. The working tree implements exactly that binding, at both ends. MINT: github-auth.guard.ts:121-127 passes `browserBinding: this.issueStateCookie(context)` into `createState`, using the same helper (:147-164) that sets the httpOnly, SameSite=Lax `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie for the web flow at :133. STORE: cli-auth.store.ts:20 and :39-45 make `browserBinding` a required, non-optional field of `StateEntry`/`CliStateParams`, so an unbound CLI state is not constructible; `consumeState` returns it at :84. CHECK: auth.controller.ts:190-208 requires `typeof binding === 'string' && secretEquals(state.browserBinding, binding)`, where `binding` is the cookie read by `takeStateCookie` (:221-228); a mismatch or absent cookie throws BadRequestException at :205. The described attack dies at steps 3-4: the victim's browser never received the attacker's `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie, so `verifyCallbackState` (called at :120, BEFORE `findOrCreateUser` at :124) rejects before any user is resolved and before the redirect to 127.0.0.1:P at :145. Call-site enumeration shows no bypassing path: the only production `createState` call site is github-auth.guard.ts:121 and the only production `consumeState` call site is auth.controller.ts:191 (every other hit is in *.spec.ts). Tests assert the precise defense said to be missing: github-auth.guard.spec.ts:153-163 ("binds a CLI login to the browser that started it") and auth.controller.spec.ts:262-279 / :281-296 (refuses a CLI callback from a different browser / with no state cookie, asserting findOrCreateUser is never reached). The reviewer's own proposed fix -- "give the CLI state the same cookie half the web state now gets" -- is already implemented verbatim in the cited file.

finding.summary: The authorization URL carrying both login bindings (nonce + PKCE challenge) is printed to stderr on browser-open failure, which is exactly the headless/agent case; an observer of that log can hijack the pending login
finding.evidence:
`console.error(oauthUrl)` at login.ts:80 emits `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>&code_challenge=<challenge>`. The comment at login.ts:52-59 and docs/design/cli.md acknowledge that anyone who reads this URL can start their own login under the same nonce and challenge and push the resulting code at the port — and because the victim's CLI holds the matching verifier, it will happily redeem the attacker's code (cli-auth.store.ts:127-132 accepts it: the challenge matches). Result: the terminal is logged into the attacker's account and every subsequent `wafflebase` write lands in the attacker's workspace.

The mitigation chosen (print only when `open` fails) inverts against the CLI's stated audience: headless CI and agent harnesses are precisely where `open` fails and where stderr is captured verbatim into logs and issue reports. The window is the 5-minute state TTL. A binding that survives disclosure of the start URL — e.g. printing only a short user_code and having the CLI hold a secret it never puts on the URL (RFC 8628 device flow), or deriving the nonce from a value the CLI never transmits — would close it.

verdict.reason: The finding asserts `console.error(oauthUrl)` fires on browser-open failure — "exactly the headless/agent case" — leaking nonce+PKCE challenge into captured stderr. The repository code is the inverse. login.ts:80 is `body: JSON.stringify({ code, codeVerifier })`, not a URL print. `openBrowser()` (login.ts:176-184) swallows every failure and returns void, so nothing branches on open success/failure; `announceLoginUrl(oauthUrl)` (login.ts:62) runs unconditionally. That function (login.ts:199-230) prints the URL to stderr ONLY under `if (process.stderr.isTTY)` (login.ts:200, print at login.ts:205). In the non-TTY case — pipes, CI logs, agent harness transcripts, i.e. the exact scenario the finding describes — the URL is never written to stderr: it is placed in `login-url.txt`, unlinked first then created with `{ mode: 0o600 }` (login.ts:210-215), and only the path plus a "one-time login secrets / expires in 5 minutes" warning is printed (login.ts:216-220). If the write throws, the fallback prints no URL at all and redirects the user to a terminal or `--api-key` (login.ts:222-228). The caller deletes the file the moment the flow settles (login.ts:68-73). The comment the finding cites as an admission is misattributed: login.ts:52-59 is the nonce/PKCE construction, while the actual doc comment at login.ts:186-198 states the opposite of the claimed behavior. A repo-wide grep for `oauthUrl|announceLoginUrl|login-url` shows no other emitter outside login.ts and its test. cli-auth.store.ts:120-139 is quoted accurately (and further refuses the no-challenge downgrade at 128-130), but that redemption path is only exploitable given the URL leak the finding alleges, and that leak vector is not present as described.

finding.summary: `/auth` access-log redaction is case- and normalization-sensitive while Express routing is not, so login secrets can still land in the access log
finding.evidence: `logSafeUrl` gates on `/^\/auth(?:\/|$)/.test(path)` (app.module.ts:39), an exact, lowercase, literal prefix test on the raw `req.url`. Express's router defaults to `case sensitive routing: false`, so `GET /AUTH/github?mode=cli&nonce=…&code_challenge=…` and `GET /Auth/github/callback?code=…&state=…` are routed to `AuthController` exactly as the lowercase forms are, but neither matches the redaction regex — the full query string (the CLI's nonce and challenge outbound, GitHub's `code` and `state` inbound) is written verbatim to the access log, and the comment itself notes every 4xx on these routes logs at `warn`. Matching against the resolved route (or lowercasing / normalising `path` before the test) closes it. Impact if triggered is precisely the exposure the redaction was added to prevent — a replayable login parked in the log.

verdict.reason: The finding claims the `/auth` redaction regex is applied to the raw `req.url` and is therefore case- and normalization-sensitive. The code does not do that. `isAuthPath` in packages/backend/src/logging/log-safe-url.ts percent-decodes the path (line 15), lowercases it and collapses repeated slashes (line 21), and only then applies `/^\/auth(?:\/|$)/` to the *normalized* string (line 22) — not to `req.url`. The decode is wrapped in try/catch that falls back to the raw spelling so a malformed escape errs toward redaction (lines 16-20). The cited location app.module.ts:39 contains no regex at all; it is a comment inside the autoLogging.ignore block, and the only wiring is `url: logSafeUrl(req.url)` at app.module.ts:70. The exact attack strings the finding names are covered by passing assertions: `/AUTH/github?nonce=n`, `/Auth/github/callback?code=abc`, `/%61uth/github?nonce=n` and `//auth/github?code=abc` all redact (log-safe-url.spec.ts:27-38), with negative boundaries pinned at :40-45. The described weakness is not present as stated.

finding.summary: The server still accepts CLI logins with no nonce and no code_challenge, leaving RFC 8252 §8.9 code injection fully open for any client that does not opt in
finding.evidence: Both bindings are optional server-side: `boundedToken(req.query?.nonce, 1, MAX_NONCE_LENGTH)` (github-auth.guard.ts:108) yields `undefined` when absent, the controller then emits no `state` echo (auth.controller.ts:144-146), and `consumeCode` returns the userId for an unchallenged code presented bare (cli-auth.store.ts:122-123). Any CLI that does not send the parameters — including the previously shipped one, which by the docs' own compatibility statement must keep working — is redeemed with the exact pre-change semantics: an attacker who guesses the loopback port pushes `http://127.0.0.1:P/callback?code=<attacker's code>` and the old CLI exchanges it, logging the terminal into the attacker's account. The guard's own bounds are also asymmetric: a malformed `code_challenge` is a 400 (line 101-103) but a malformed/over-long `nonce` is silently dropped (line 108), producing an unbound login the client believes is bound. Consider making both mandatory for `mode=cli` (or gating the legacy path behind an explicit opt-in) once the CLI version floor allows it, and treating a present-but-malformed `nonce` the same way as a malformed challenge.

verdict.reason: The code is not as described. In this tree `GitHubAuthGuard` makes BOTH CLI bindings mandatory: `github-auth.guard.ts:106-109` throws `BadRequestException('Missing or invalid nonce')` when `boundedToken(req.query?.nonce, 1, MAX_NONCE_LENGTH)` is undefined (absent, non-string, or over-long — so a malformed nonce is a 400, not a silent drop), and `github-auth.guard.ts:111-119` throws for a missing/malformed `code_challenge`. The claimed asymmetry and the claimed optional bindings do not exist. The controller's nonce echo is unconditional (`auth.controller.ts:144-147`), not omitted, and `nonce`/`codeChallenge` are non-optional fields of `CliStateParams` (`cli-auth.store.ts:39-45`). The only production caller of `createCode` is `auth.controller.ts:140`, which always passes `cliState.codeChallenge`, so the legacy `!entry.codeChallenge` branch at `cli-auth.store.ts:128-129` cannot be reached by any server-minted code. Entry-point sweep: `createState` has exactly one production caller (`github-auth.guard.ts:121`), and `GitHubAuthGuard` is the sole guard on `GET /auth/github` (`auth.controller.ts:94-95`), with `github.strategy.ts:61-67` merely forwarding `__oauthState`; no alternate route can start an unbound CLI login. The described exploit chain (old CLI redeeming an attacker-pushed bare code) requires a state created without nonce/challenge, which the guard refuses.
